title: Why Are Bananas Still So Cheap?

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: Walk into any supermarket today, and you will quickly notice almost everything costs significantly more than it used to. Yet tucked away in the produce aisle, one favorite staple seems almost completely immune to modern inflation.

segments.label: scene 2 (counter)
segments.text: Since January 2000, overall US grocery prices nearly doubled, jumping 95%.

segments.label: scene 3 (compare)
segments.text: For example, white bread skyrocketed 105%, going from $0.91 per pound in January 2000 to $1.86 by October 2026.

segments.label: scene 4 (line)
segments.text: A gallon of whole milk climbed 47% across that same timeframe, rising to $4.10.

segments.label: scene 5 (bars)
segments.text: Meanwhile, banana prices rose just 34% from January 2000 to October 2026.

segments.label: scene 6 (multiline)
segments.text: Back in January 2000, bananas cost $0.49 a pound, and by October 2026, they reached just $0.66.

segments.label: scene 7 (gauge)
segments.text: Even when checking where prices sit today relative to historical ranges, bananas remain remarkably frozen in time. How has this fragile tropical fruit defied global supply shocks for a quarter century?

segments.label: scene 8 (line)
segments.text: To understand this stability, look at how little the price moved over twenty-six years. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, bananas dropped to a low of $0.47 in November 2004.

segments.label: scene 9 (gauge)
segments.text: Even at their peak in September 2025, bananas reached just $0.67 per pound. That creates a price range of just twenty cents across a quarter century.

segments.label: scene 10 (compare)
segments.text: In January 2010, bananas cost $0.59 per pound. By January 2020, they fell to $0.57.

segments.label: scene 11 (counter)
segments.text: Spikes were rare. In February 2009, prices jumped 19% in a single year to hit $0.64.

segments.label: scene 12 (statement)
segments.text: Ultra-efficient supply chains and supermarket pricing strategies keep retail costs frozen.

segments.label: scene 13 (bars)
segments.text: Since January 2010, banana prices rose just 12%. Over that same span, overall grocery prices climbed 50% and white bread rose 37%.

segments.label: scene 14 (multiline)
segments.text: Over the last year from November 2025 to October 2026, banana prices fell 1.4%, even as milk peaked at $4.32 in June 2026.

segments.label: scene 15 (line)
segments.text: Consider what happened to white bread over that same quarter century. By October 2026, its average price reached 2.1 times its starting level in January 2000.

segments.label: scene 16 (line)
segments.text: Bread prices hit a record peak of $2.03 per pound in January 2024. Even over the last year, bread managed a +4.0% bump.

segments.label: scene 17 (counter)
segments.text: Whole milk followed a similarly turbulent path across American grocery stores. Back in March 2003, a gallon dropped to a low of $2.66.

segments.label: scene 18 (counter)
segments.text: Milk later surged to $4.22 per gallon in November 2022 after climbing +15% in just twelve months.

segments.label: scene 19 (bars)
segments.text: Looking back to January 2005, white bread surged +87% and whole milk gained +24%.

segments.label: scene 20 (slope)
segments.text: Yet over that exact same span from January 2005 to October 2026, banana prices rose just +35%.

segments.label: scene 21 (statement)
segments.text: Why do basic bakery and dairy items fluctuate wildly while tropical fruit pricing remains remarkably tethered?

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: Supermarkets strategically keep banana prices artificially low to attract store traffic. Retailers treat the fresh fruit as a primary loss leader.

segments.label: scene 23 (multiline)
segments.text: Since 2005, overall grocery costs jumped 71%. Yet bananas stayed far more stable than dairy or bakery items over that same stretch.

segments.label: scene 24 (counter)
segments.text: White bread traded at $1.00 per pound in January 2005. Retailers willingly accept razor-thin produce margins while marking up packaged goods.

segments.label: scene 25 (statement)
segments.text: Beyond retail strategy, global logistics shield tropical fruit. Optimized cold chain container ships and rigid supply contracts insulate importers from cost swings.

segments.label: scene 26 (line)
segments.text: Other fresh foods face volatile domestic inputs. Whole milk reached $3.76 per gallon in January 2015 as feed and energy costs surged.

segments.label: scene 27 (line)
segments.text: Since 2015, total grocery prices expanded 33%. Over that same period, white bread gained 26%, while whole milk grew 9%.

segments.label: scene 28 (counter)
segments.text: By January 2025, bananas averaged just $0.62 per pound. Highly integrated supply chains keep landed costs remarkably steady.

segments.label: scene 29 (slope)
segments.text: For household budgets, post-2020 price divergences created a dramatic split across standard grocery aisles, reshaping weekly shopping bills.

segments.label: scene 30 (line)
segments.text: Take white bread, which stood at $1.35 back in January 2020. Driven by surging food processing, logistics, and energy expenses, white bread prices jumped 38% through October 2026.

segments.label: scene 31 (counter)
segments.text: Across the entire store, overall grocery costs climbed 32% post-2020, steadily eroding real purchasing power for everyday working families.

segments.label: scene 32 (bars)
segments.text: When you compare these major kitchen staples on one chart, tropical produce visibly decouples from volatile domestic agricultural benchmarks.

segments.label: scene 33 (slope)
segments.text: Whole milk sat at $3.25 per gallon in January 2020 before elevated feed costs, dairy processing, and distribution pushed prices higher.

segments.label: scene 34 (statement)
segments.text: Because grocery stores treat fresh bananas as key loss leaders, stable banana pricing actively counterbalances inflation on essential packaged goods.

segments.label: scene 35 (kpi)
segments.text: This predictable price tag provides a vital buffer for lower-income shoppers, proving that store strategy can shield key family staples.

segments.label: scene 36 (multiline)
segments.text: Looking back across more than two decades, the contrast across grocery aisles remains staggering. While standard white bread more than doubled in cost, yellow bananas stayed remarkably grounded.

segments.label: scene 37 (statement)
segments.text: Retailers continuously sacrificed produce margins, using low pricing to attract foot traffic while marking up processed goods.

segments.label: scene 38 (compare)
segments.text: Even during recent pullbacks, when white bread dropped 8% from its record peak, packaged staples remained far higher than their historic baselines.

segments.label: scene 39 (line)
segments.text: Meanwhile, whole milk eased 5% from its June 2026 high, yet dairy costs still fluctuated far more than imported fruit.

segments.label: scene 40 (statement)
segments.text: Ultimately, tight supply chains and deliberate store pricing shielded an essential fruit, proving that retail strategy can buffer consumers from broad inflation.
